quote: And—may I ask?
why: Elizabeth announces a question and then never asks one; the next sentence opens with 'But', so the line reads as broken off rather than hesitant.
suggestion: And—may I ask—the terms, I suppose, must be accepted?

quote: In terms of grateful acknowledgment for his brother's kindness, though expressed as briefly as possible, he then set down on paper
why: 'In terms of' is used where 'in' or 'with' is meant, so the opening clause doesn't attach to anything and the sentence has to be re-read.
suggestion: In a brief note of grateful thanks for his brother's kindness, he then set down on paper

quote: He would be scarcely ten pounds a year worse off by the hundred that was to be paid them
why: The arithmetic (paying out £100 a year costs him barely £10 more than Lydia already cost him) is packed into a compressed phrase that listeners will lose.
suggestion: Paying them the hundred a year would leave him scarcely ten pounds a year worse off than before

quote: That his anger could reach such a point of unimaginable resentment as to deny his daughter a privilege without which her marriage would hardly seem real exceeded everything she thought possible.
why: A long noun-clause subject ('That his anger ... real') holds the verb back to the very end; readers lose the thread before 'exceeded' arrives.
suggestion: She could not believe his anger could go so far as to deny his daughter something without which her marriage would hardly seem real.

quote: Not, however, from any fear of personal harm to herself
why: 'Personal harm' suggests physical danger; what is meant is that she had nothing to lose, since her hopes of Darcy were already gone.
suggestion: Not, however, because she had anything to lose by it herself

quote: a family to whose existing objections would now be added an alliance with the man he most justly despised
why: The inverted relative clause ('to whose existing objections would now be added') is hard to parse aloud.
suggestion: a family that already had its drawbacks and would now also be related to the man he most justly despised

quote: His daughter's request—for such it might be considered—to be welcomed back into the family before heading north was initially met with a flat refusal.
why: The paragraph before is Mrs. Bennet speaking, so 'His' has no near antecedent; Mr. Bennet is only identified later by 'urged him'.
suggestion: Lydia's request—for such it might be considered—to be welcomed back into the family before heading north was at first flatly refused by her father.

quote: Elizabeth was forced to put it out of her power by running away
why: 'Put it out of her power' (to ask) is a period construction, and 'it' has no clear referent.
suggestion: Elizabeth had to run away so that she couldn't ask

quote: he'd been forced to leave the regiment because of pressing debts of honor
why: 'Debts of honor' (gambling debts, not legally enforceable) will be misread as something honorable; the meaning matters to Wickham's character.
suggestion: because of pressing gambling debts

quote: that's the living I ought to have had
why: 'Living' in the sense of a church post with its income is unfamiliar to most modern readers; 'rectory' helps, but only after the fact.
suggestion: that's the church living—the parish post—I ought to have had

quote: Had she not seen him in Derbyshire, she might have supposed he was coming with no intention beyond what was openly stated
why: The previous paragraph is Jane speaking of Bingley, but Darcy is the man most associated with Derbyshire, so 'him' is briefly ambiguous until 'his friend's permission'.
suggestion: Had she not seen Bingley in Derbyshire, she might have supposed he was coming with no intention beyond what was openly stated

quote: People did say you meant to leave the place entirely at Michaelmas
why: Michaelmas (late September, a quarter-day when leases ended) is unfamiliar; the meaning is recoverable but a gloss helps.
suggestion: People did say you meant to give up the house entirely at Michaelmas, when the lease was up

quote: He appeared nobly indifferent; and she would have imagined Bingley had received Darcy's blessing to be happy, had she not seen his eyes also turn toward Mr. Darcy with an expression of half-amused alarm.
why: 'He' is Darcy, then 'his eyes' switch to Bingley without warning, so for a moment Darcy seems to be looking at himself.
suggestion: He appeared nobly indifferent; and she would have imagined Bingley had received Darcy's blessing to be happy, had she not seen Bingley's own eyes turn toward Mr. Darcy with an expression of half-amused alarm.

quote: Anxious and restless, the period in the drawing room before the gentlemen arrived was tedious and dull to a degree that almost made her rude.
why: Dangling modifier: 'Anxious and restless' grammatically describes 'the period', not Elizabeth.
suggestion: Anxious and restless, she found the time in the drawing room before the gentlemen arrived so tedious and dull that it almost made her rude.

quote: she went upstairs half an hour ago
why: The sisters are already upstairs, so 'went upstairs' doesn't explain why Kitty is 'ahead of us'; it means she went up to dress earlier.
suggestion: she went up to dress half an hour ago

quote: with a patience and composure particularly grateful to the daughter
why: 'Grateful' in the old sense of 'pleasing' reads as though the daughter's gratitude were being described in the wrong place.
suggestion: with a patience and composure that the daughter particularly appreciated

quote: The latter was much more agreeable than his companion had expected. There was nothing foolish or presumptuous about Bingley to provoke his ridicule or put him off; and he was more talkative and less eccentric than Mr. Bennet had ever seen him.
why: 'The latter' is Mr. Bennet (more agreeable than Bingley expected), but the last clause says Bingley was more talkative and 'less eccentric' than Mr. Bennet had seen him, which reverses the logic; 'eccentric' only fits Mr. Bennet. The passage contradicts itself.
suggestion: Mr. Bennet was much more agreeable than Bingley had expected. There was nothing foolish or presumptuous about Bingley to provoke his ridicule or put him off; and Mr. Bennet was more talkative and less eccentric than Bingley had ever seen him.

quote: she wouldn't be missed to counteract her mother's plots
why: 'Wouldn't be missed to counteract' is not idiomatic. The meaning is that her presence wasn't needed to counter her mother's schemes.
suggestion: she wasn't needed to counteract her mother's plots

quote: there seemed to be a rather pretty little wilderness on one side of your lawn
why: 'Wilderness' as a planted, deliberately informal area of garden is a period term; modern readers picture wild land. (The 'hermitage' in 56.17 raises the same issue.)
suggestion: there seemed to be a rather pretty little wooded garden on one side of your lawn

quote: "You can now have nothing further to say," she answered angrily.
why: The previous paragraph is Lady Catherine's speech, so 'she' could be either woman on first hearing, especially aloud.
suggestion: "You can now have nothing further to say," Elizabeth answered angrily.

quote: she added
why: Nothing has been spoken before this, since the previous paragraphs are narrated thought, so 'added' has nothing to add to.
suggestion: she thought

quote: dwelling on every word of the latter which, in her Ladyship's view, showed particular defiance and audacity, in the belief that such a report would help her obtain from her nephew the promise Elizabeth had refused to give
why: A long sentence already carries two clauses when 'the latter' and a trailing 'in the belief that' clause are added; the chain of referents is hard to follow.
suggestion: She had dwelt on every word of Elizabeth's that seemed to her particularly defiant and audacious, believing this would help her get from her nephew the promise Elizabeth had refused to give.

quote: you must be married by special license
why: 'Special license' (an expensive permission to marry anywhere, at any time, without banns) is unfamiliar; Mrs. Bennet's point is that it is a status symbol.
suggestion: you must be married by special license, like the grandest people

quote: seeing Mr. Darcy subjected to all the fawning and obsequious politeness of her husband
why: The subject of the sentence is Elizabeth, so 'her husband' reads at first as Elizabeth's husband (Darcy), not Charlotte's (Mr. Collins).
suggestion: seeing Mr. Darcy subjected to all the fawning and obsequious politeness of Charlotte's husband

quote: even after peace was restored
why: This means the end of the war, which frees Wickham from the army, but it reads as peace within the family.
suggestion: even after the war ended

quote: from the visits of her uncle and aunt from the city
why: The sentence's subject is Lady Catherine, so 'her uncle and aunt' reads as hers rather than Elizabeth's. 'From the city' (London trade) also carries the snobbery and needs to land.
suggestion: from the visits of Elizabeth's uncle and aunt, who were in trade in London
